name: Hadza

ancestors.notes: Hadza is a language isolate (Glottolog hadz1240); the clade node represents its own one-member family.

notes: Language isolate of Tanzania (Glottolog hadz1240) with a three-place click series. This map follows the practical orthography of the Miller/Anyawire Hadza lexicon (Miller 2008; Miller & Anyawire et al. 2013), which is the convention the available Hadza word lists are written in. Its defining choices: the dental, alveolar and lateral clicks are written ⟨c q x⟩ rather than with the click letters, so ⟨c⟩=[k͡ǀ], ⟨q⟩=[k͡ǃ], ⟨x⟩=[k͡ǁ]; ⟨h⟩ after a click letter marks aspiration (⟨ch qh xh⟩); a preceding ⟨n⟩ marks the nasal click (⟨nc nq nx⟩); and DOUBLING the letter marks the glottalised nasal click (⟨cc qq xx⟩). The same doubling convention carries the ejective/affricate series outside the clicks: ⟨bb⟩=[pʼ], ⟨jj⟩=[t͡ʃʼ], ⟨zz⟩=[t͡sʼ], ⟨gg⟩=[k͡xʼ] and labialised ⟨ggw⟩=[k͡xʷʼ] (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996 for the inventory these letters spell). The doubled letters are built on the VOICED letter of each pair, and that voiced letter keeps its own value: single ⟨z⟩ is [d͡z] and single ⟨j⟩ is [d͡ʒ] (the [t͡ʃ] it shows in the attested words is the general post-nasal devoicing, not the phoneme). No ⟨dd⟩ is mapped: /tʼ/ is not in the described inventory, and the letter appears only in the alphabet table, never in a word. ⟨hh⟩ is the velar fricative [x] and single ⟨h⟩ the breathy glottal [ɦ]; ⟨r⟩ is the lateral flap [ɺ] (Sands 2013). The sources are not fully agreed here: Sands 2013 names a lateral flap, while the phonetic descriptions of the same segment elsewhere in the literature treat it as a plain alveolar tap [ɾ] whose laterality is a transition off the flanking vowels rather than a contrastive feature. [ɺ] is used because it is the value the handbook chapter states outright; a spec that wanted [ɾ] would not be contradicting a settled fact. ⟨tl tlh dl⟩ are the palatal lateral affricate series [c͡ʎ̥˔], [c͡ʎ̥˔ʰ], [c͡ʎ̥˔ʼ] — the ejective member is voiceless like the other two; ⟨sl⟩ is the lateral fricative [ɬ]. A marginal bilabial click survives in a handful of items and is written ⟨mc⟩ / labialised ⟨mcw⟩ = [ᵑʘ], [ᵑʘʷ] (Sands 2013). Vowel length is written with a circumflex (⟨â ê î ô û⟩ = [aː eː iː oː uː]). Every vowel-initial word takes a predictable glottal onset [ʔ], and a hiatus between two written vowels is broken by [ʔ] as well — Hadza has no vowel-initial syllable and no true vowel sequence (Sands 2013, §syllable structure; Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996). Word-initial ⟨y⟩ spells that same glottal-onset plus high front vowel [ʔi]. Between vowels, ⟨y⟩ and ⟨w⟩ are the written separator of a TRUE vowel sequence rather than consonants of their own — Sands 2013 (fn. 7) calls the [j] and [w] so written mere transitions between the flanking vowels — so they do not take the hiatus [ʔ], and the transition itself is absent whenever a flanking vowel already shares the glide's place: ⟨y⟩ deletes next to a front vowel, ⟨w⟩ next to a round vowel. With neither neighbour matching, the transition is audible and is written. Nasal vowels are NOT part of this orthography: a written ⟨n⟩ after a vowel is a nasal consonant, not a nasalisation mark. Pitch and stress are not encoded and are not modelled here.

sources.notes: Instrumental description of the Hadza consonant inventory: the click series and its nasal/glottalised members, the ejective series built on the voiced letters of the orthography (pʼ t͡sʼ t͡ʃʼ k͡xʼ and the lateral c͡ʎ̥˔ʼ), the lateral obstruents, and the absence of voiced obstruents after a nasal. Source for the phoneme values behind the doubled-letter and post-nasal rules. NOTE: no /tʼ/ is described for Hadza — the alphabet-row spelling ⟨dd⟩ is not mapped here for want of a source.

allophone_rules.notes: Post-nasal stop devoicing: the orthographic voiced stop of ⟨mb⟩ ⟨nd⟩ ⟨ng⟩ is phonetically voiceless. Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996 (The phonetic structures of Hadza, UCLA WPP 91 / Studies in African Linguistics 25) report that Hadza has no voiced stop after a nasal; the nasal+stop sequence is realised with a plain voiceless stop.
Post-nasal stop devoicing, coronal member of the same series (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996).
Post-nasal stop devoicing, velar member of the same series (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996).

Post-nasal stop devoicing, the palato-alveolar affricate member of the same series: ⟨nj⟩ is [nt͡ʃ]. Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996 (The phonetic structures of Hadza, Studies in African Linguistics 25(2), 171-204): Hadza has no voiced obstruent after a nasal.

Post-nasal aspiration: where the orthography writes the plain voiceless letter after a nasal (⟨nt⟩), the stop is aspirated — the contrast ⟨nd⟩ [nt] vs ⟨nt⟩ [ntʰ] is what the two spellings encode (Sands 2013, 'Hadza', in Vossen ed., The Khoesan Languages, Routledge, §phonology; Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996).
Post-nasal aspiration, velar member: ⟨nk⟩ [nkʰ] against ⟨ng⟩ [nk] (Sands 2013; Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996).

Post-nasal aspiration, labial member: ⟨mp⟩ is [mpʰ], the labial counterpart of the ⟨nt⟩/⟨nk⟩ contrast against ⟨nd⟩/⟨ng⟩ (Sands 2013, 'Hadza', in Vossen ed., The Khoesan Languages, Routledge). The documented series is complete at all three places; this member happens not to be exercised by any word in the current hts gold, which is a fact about the gold, not about Hadza.
Post-nasal aspiration extends to the coronal affricate: ⟨nts⟩ [ntʰs]~[nt͡sʰ] (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996, affricate series).

Hiatus-breaking glide, not a phoneme. Sands 2013 ('Hadza', in Vossen ed., The Khoesan Languages, Routledge) describes ⟨y⟩ and ⟨w⟩ between vowels as the written separator of a true vowel sequence, and states (fn. 7) that the [j] and [w] so written are mere transitions between the flanking vowels rather than segments. The transition is therefore absent — the two vowels are simply adjacent — exactly when one of the flanking vowels already shares the glide's own place: a front vowel for ⟨y⟩, a round vowel for ⟨w⟩. With neither neighbour matching, the transition is audible and is transcribed.
